frus-1863p2:
Part II of the 1863 foreign affairs papers ranges across the whole diplomatic map. France fills the largest block of documents. Russia, the Netherlands, and China follow. Spain, Austria, and Prussia have their own sections. Japan takes a long run of papers. Smaller sections cover Italy, Belgium, and Turkey. Egypt, Morocco, Mexico, and Brazil also appear.

The French papers show the Civil War pressing on every tie. Seward answers a French offer of mediation with refusal. The Confederate raider Alabama appears in the first letters. Reports from Paris track plots to detach Texas. A supplement adds more French papers. Consular letters from British and European ports close the volume. It is the Union's wartime diplomacy in raw form.
frus-1864p2:
Part II of the 1864 papers stays with Great Britain. The first block continues the main correspondence. An appendix and the British legation's letters follow. Seward and Adams write on neutrality debates in Parliament. The Laird rams and the Alexandra still lead the agenda. The cruiser Georgia is advertised for sale and watched.

Confederate sea power threads through the whole volume. One report follows Captain Semmes and the Alabama off South Africa. His ship boards British merchantmen near the Cape. Forged calls for volunteers and public opinion also appear. The legation papers handle claims and protests in Washington. Together the two blocks show a daily diplomatic grind. Nothing here is settled, but war with Britain is kept off.
frus-1865p2:
In Part II of the 1865 papers, the British legation writes from Washington. Its letters open the volume. France and the French legation follow. Russia, the Netherlands, China, and Spain complete it. The legation file bristles with wartime incidents. Confederate schemes in Canada fill many pages. The Shenandoah and the St. Albans raiders appear.

Lincoln's death breaks into the French section. Bigelow reports Paris in mourning that May. A Bonaparte prince writes his sympathy to Seward. Spain's file closes the volume with its own claims. The papers mix high grief with petty friction. Border raids, coal claims, and extradition requests crowd together. It is diplomacy at street level in a war's last year.
frus-1866p2:
Prussia leads Part II of the 1866 foreign affairs papers. Wright reports from Berlin as Bismarck faces the Chambers. Naturalized Americans held for Prussian military service fill many letters. The Schleswig-Holstein question pushes Prussia and Austria toward war. Belgium, Portugal, and Italy follow. Rome, Denmark, and Switzerland have brief files. Japan and Turkey extend the volume eastward.

The second half turns to the Americas. Argentina, Brazil, and Chile open a long Latin American run. Peru and Paraguay close it. A Chilean file catches Spain's Pacific war. One report describes an admiral checking his orders on arbitration mid-interview. An appendix returns to Japan. The volume shows American diplomacy after Appomattox. Its reach is now fully global.
frus-1867p2:
Turkey opens Part II of the 1867 papers, far from the volume's center of gravity. Morris reports an earthquake on Mitylene. Seward protests harsh laws against Jews in Servia. Congress sends sympathy to the people of Crete. Japan, Egypt, and Tunis follow in short files. Then the correspondence crosses the Atlantic. Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia, and Chile lead a long American run.

Mexico swells to the largest share. Its legation papers match the main file in weight. The mid-volume reports describe Maximilian's capture at Queretaro. A French minister seeks passage to plead for the prisoner. The besiegers refuse, and mediation fails. Peru, Paraguay, and Colombia close the book. Two hemispheres share one binding theme. Small states and great claims crowd every post.
frus-1868p2:
Part II of the 1868 papers begins with Spain and a quarantine quarrel. Seward holds Spain answerable for damage to American ships. Washington also offers mediation in Spain's war with South American states. The North German Union and Austria follow. Italy, Belgium, Denmark, and Portugal have short files. Greece and Egypt add Mediterranean color.

The Americas fill the second half. Mexico takes a long run of papers. Its mid-volume debate defends harsh laws against bandits in Jalisco. Paraguay gets an appendix of its own. Peru and Venezuela close the volume with legation files. Colombia ends the list. The range is the widest yet in the series. Routine consular business sits beside wars and claims.
frus-1888p2:
Part II of the 1888 papers completes the alphabet and adds supplements. Italy through Venezuela fill the country list. Mexico takes the longest run, with its legation file behind. Turkey and Switzerland follow in size. Then five supplements break the country pattern. The first prints the Lord Sackville case. The second revives the 1886 extradition treaty papers.

Bering Sea dominates the third supplement. It prints seizures of British sealing vessels. A fourth seeks treaties to protect the fur seals. France, Germany, Japan, and Russia all join that file. A fifth supplement weighs differential tonnage dues. Treaty claims from six legations crowd its pages. A Norwegian letter, mid-volume, defends its district on leper emigration. Supplements make this part a small archive.
frus-1894app2:
Appendix II to the 1894 papers is a Hawaii archive. It binds several Senate and House documents together. The first transmits a draft of an uncompleted treaty. The second traces American relations with Hawaii since 1820. A formal report covers consular ties from their start. The annexation treaty of February 14, 1893 follows. Cleveland's own Hawaiian message appears in full.

Instructions to Minister Willis fill another document. Correspondence since March 1889 accompanies them. Affidavits form a part of their own. Mid-volume testimony answers questions about troops. Witnesses recall Sunday talk of landing forces for safety. Annexation's supporters wished for American troops ashore. The volume lets readers judge the revolution's record. Two presidents' policies stand side by side.
frus-1895p2:
Part II of the 1895 papers picks up at Greece. Hawaii takes its largest share. Political events there fill a long run. Neutrality charges and a minister's recall follow. Italy's file turns on blood in Colorado. Italian laborers were killed there, and Rome protests. Honduras prints a murder case, the death of Charles Renton.

Korea stands between Japan and Mexico in the list. Its independence and political events get two headings. Mexico argues its boundary with Guatemala. Nicaragua faces British demands in its file. The Mosquito Territory's incorporation closes that story. A Russian letter, mid-volume, presses one citizen's discharge. The legation holds his case, it says, and pushes for release. Part II balances islands and isthmuses. Old annexation questions meet new claims.
frus-1902app2:
Appendix II of 1902 prints the Pious Fund case against Mexico. Jackson Ralston, the American agent, reports the award. His report leads, with the award in translation. Pleadings follow in three languages. The American memorial states the claim in English. Mexico answers in Spanish; a French response joins it. The fund had supported California missions long before.

Its assets passed through sales and decrees over decades. A decree of October 1842 ordered the properties sold. Interest owed after that sale fills the mid-volume arithmetic. Treaties and claims conventions crowd the appendix. They run from the peace treaty to the 1868 commission. The volume is a complete arbitration record. Church money becomes a question between nations.
frus-1906p2:
Part II of the 1906 papers runs from Haiti onward. Haiti expels foreigners and withdraws consular exequaturs. Syrian-born Americans need licenses there, one file notes. Italy's section erupts with Mount Vesuvius. The eruption fills a run of relief papers. Harsh treatment of Italian laborers follows. A counterfeited American consular seal draws protest. Passport rulings fill the legal pages between.

An infant may receive a passport, one heading rules. Foreign names get anglicized in naturalization papers. Russia supplies the mid-volume analysis. Its Duma electoral colleges are dissected by class. Peasant electors hold a special privilege, the report says. Workmen may elect no member of their own. The part mixes islands, volcanoes, and parliaments. Bureaucracy is its true subject.
frus-1907p2:
Central America commands Part II of the 1907 papers. Guatemala impresses aliens into its army, one file protests. An attempt on Guatemala's president follows. The United States and Mexico then offer good offices. Their joint peace work fills the part's bulk. A peace protocol signed at Washington in September follows. The Central American Peace Conference reports in full. Honduras gains recognition for its provisional government.

Haiti taxes and mistreats in its smaller file. Japan signs treaties with France and Russia. The mid-volume text quotes the Hague rules for hospital ships. Such vessels escape dues in contracting ports during war. The part is a peace conference's archive. Two presidents act as the isthmus's sponsors.
frus-1948v01p2:
Part 2 of Volume I for 1948 turns from UN housekeeping to broad policy. Threat studies, military posture, aid abroad, and base rights lead the record. Atomic energy's foreign side follows in its own block.

Trade takes the largest share, with the Havana meeting on a world trade body and the first GATT sessions. Credit policy, trade treaties, and tax accords fill shorter runs. Aid totals and Antarctic claims close the part. The papers show a state building world rules for trade while it armed for a long rivalry. Aid ran to many lands that year.
frus-1948v05p2:
Part 2 of Volume V for 1948 is given over to one subject: Palestine and the birth of Israel. Hundreds of papers run from the partition debate at the United Nations to the creation of the state. The entry of Arab forces and the first war follow in cables and memos.

An appendix prints Resolution 181, the partition plan adopted on November 29, 1947. Truce bids, refugee questions, and Jerusalem's fate fill the later runs. The record is day by day and often hour by hour. Few single-topic parts in the series match its depth.
frus-1949v07p2:
Part 2 of Volume VII for 1949 turns to Northeast Asia. Japan's occupation and control lead the record, with policy papers on its future. Korea follows, as American forces withdrew and aid to the Republic of Korea grew.

The Korean question at the United Nations takes its own run. A closing block weighs policy for the whole East Asia-Pacific area, with talk of regional pacts. The papers show planners shifting from occupation duties to alliance building. Within a year, Korea would test every choice recorded here. Pact talk shows how fast the map was redrawn.
frus-1951v03p2:
Part 2 of Volume III for 1951 stays with the German question. Study group work on banned industries and the occupation statute leads. Draft deals to set West Germany on a contract basis follow in detail.

Money for defense, safety controls, and unity bids fill the middle runs. Berlin access and trade pacts show the city's weak spot. The Saar and reports from the Soviet zone close the part. The record shows a half-state being armed, funded, and bound to the West, while unity stayed a slogan for both sides. Rearmament's pace is the measure argued in nearly every paper here.
frus-1951v04p2:
Part 2 of Volume IV for 1951 turns to Central and Eastern Europe. Austria leads, with occupation costs, aid, and the stalled state treaty. Talk of a future Austrian army appears near the end of its block.

East Europe follows, on treaty duties, exile groups, and Soviet peace drives. The Oatis case in Czechoslovakia and the Vogeler case in Hungary mark the low point in ties. Reports from behind the frontier show states sealed off. Each file pairs a formal protest with a plain lack of means to change the facts. Manpower and money are weighed together in the closing staff papers.
frus-1951v06p2:
Part 2 of Volume VI for 1951 turns to South Asia, after short runs on New Zealand, the Philippines, and Thailand. Kashmir dominates, with hundreds of papers on bids to settle the India-Pakistan dispute. The Pushtunistan row between Afghanistan and Pakistan follows.

India takes the closing block, on emergency aid and its stance between East and West. Ceylon's rubber sales to Communist China also appear. Pakistan's problems fill the final files. The record shows a new subcontinent whose quarrels at once drew in the wider rivalry, despite Delhi's wish to stand apart.
frus-1951v07p2:
Part 2 of Volume VII for 1951 turns to the China area. Policy toward the People's Republic and ties with the Republic of China on Formosa fill the main block. Aid flows, Tibet's fate, and jailed Americans all appear.

Trade curbs form the second block, with UN sanctions on North Korea and mainland China. Papers weigh how tight the embargo should be and who must enforce it. The record shows two Chinas treated as a war problem and a trade problem at once, with Formosa's shield at the center of each choice.
frus-1952-54v01p2:
Part 2 of Volume I for 1952–1954 opens with economic defense. Controls on East-West trade, stockpiles of key goods, and guarding key industries fill the first block. Antitrust action against the world oil firms follows.

Loyalty probes in Congress and their foreign fallout take the next run. Migration, the law of the sea, and Antarctic claims sit in shorter sections. The Bricker bid to curb treaty power closes the part. The papers show home politics and world policy shaping each other, file by file, across three crowded years. Each fight left a paper trail of memos.
frus-1952-54v02p2:
Part 2 of Volume II for 1952–1954 turns to atomic energy and arms control. President Eisenhower's Atoms for Peace proposal of December 8, 1953, anchors the record. Talks on sharing atomic work for peaceful ends fill long runs.

War scare talks with Britain and Canada follow, on base use in a general war. Emergency base deals abroad sit beside them. The foreign information program closes the part, with the 1953 report on it printed in full. The papers mix the atom as threat, promise, and message in one file. Fact sheets and films carried the message to the public.
frus-1952-54v05p2:
Part 2 of Volume V for 1952–1954 opens in crisis. France had rejected the European Defense Community treaty, and the Western design hung in doubt. Eden's tour and Dulles's trips to Bonn and London fill the first block.

The Nine-Power and Four-Power meetings in London follow, told session by session. Their work put West Germany on the path to NATO entry and restored sovereignty. Minutes show bargains struck in days. The part is the record of a rescue job, done at speed, that fixed the Western map for decades. The settlement shaped Europe for a generation.
frus-1952-54v06p2:
Part 2 of Volume VI for 1952–1954 works through the allies one by one. France leads, with aid for its arms program and visits by Mayer and Mendès-France. Italy, Spain, and Portugal follow, each with base or aid deals at the core.

Iceland's defense pact and Ireland's bids for arms outside NATO sit in shorter runs. The Vatican question appears near the end. Canada closes the part, with the St. Lawrence talks. The record shows an alliance held together by side deals as much as by shared aims. Each capital's file pairs courtesy with hard bargaining.
frus-1952-54v07p2:
Part 2 of Volume VII for 1952–1954 begins with Allied rights in Berlin and the Saar's status. Reports from the Soviet zone follow, on the June 1953 unrest, food aid, and Moscow's grant of sovereignty to its German state.

Austria fills the rest of the part. Treaty bids, occupation costs, and visits by Figl and Raab to Washington mark the run. Acheson's Vienna stop also appears. Policy papers weigh smaller garrisons and a two-party state. The record ends a year before the treaty that freed Austria at last was signed. The closing files weigh Spain's bases against the alliance's wider needs.
frus-1952-54v09p2:
Part 2 of Volume IX for 1952–1954 turns to single states of the Near and Middle East. Egypt leads, with the long push for a Suez Canal Zone settlement. The Sudan accord of February 1953 and the Suez accord of October 1954 frame the run.

Iran follows, on aid and the Anglo-Iranian oil dispute. Iraq, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia fill the rest, with the Buraimi boundary fight in long detail. Yemen closes the part in two papers. The cables show base rights and oil terms being reset across the region. Aid missions report from nearly every capital in the part's final run.
frus-1952-54v11p2:
South Asia fills Part 2 of Volume XI for 1952–1954. Kashmir again dominates, with hundreds of papers on settlement bids between India and Pakistan. The Pushtunistan dispute follows, as Kabul and Karachi contested the frontier tribes.

Afghanistan and Ceylon take middle runs, on aid and on rubber and rice. India closes the part, with its stance between the blocs in long detail. Pakistan ends the volume, with wheat aid, Vice President Nixon's visit, and military aid. The record shows a region courted by both camps and split by its own quarrels. Communist pressure on the offshore islands shadows the part's closing pages.
frus-1952-54v12p2:
Country files fill Part 2 of Volume XII for 1952–1954. Burma leads, with the sore point of Chinese Nationalist troops on its soil. Indonesia follows, on aid programs and care to stay neutral on Western New Guinea.

The Philippines takes the next run, on its defense pact, its 1953 vote, and trade deal changes. Thailand closes the part, with aid rising fast. Embassy reports show small states bargaining with a patron at war's edge. Each asked for arms and cash, and each guarded its freedom to say no. Aid terms were argued as hard as arms totals.
frus-1952-54v14p2:
Japan fills Part 2 of Volume XIV for 1952–1954, as the China part's companion. Ties and policy toward Japan run in one long block, from the peace treaty's first years into the security pact's working life. Bases, costs, and trade fill the cables.

A Korean plea runs through the mid-sample: Seoul asks that its forces match Japan's and fears aid spent on Japanese goods. Washington urges both sides to look ahead. The part shows a former enemy being rebuilt as the anchor ally of the northwest Pacific, step by step. Prisoner and neutral-nations fights fill the part's closing files here.
frus-1952-54v15p2:
Part 2 of Volume XV for 1952–1954 carries Korea from armistice into an armed peace. President Rhee's solo release of prisoners opens the run, with talks halted in protest. The Robertson mission and final terms lead to the July 1953 armistice.

Rebuilding, a defense pact, and failed political talks fill the next block. Troop pullbacks, the Van Fleet mission, and Rhee's Washington visit close the part. An agreed minute on aid ends the files. The record shows a war stopped, not settled, with each side armed for its return. Aid files show the price of the new pact.
frus-1955-57v23p2:
Korea fills Part 2 of Volume XXIII of the 1955–1957 set. Two linked fights run through the whole part. The first seeks the removal of the Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission from Korea. The second weighs bringing advanced weapons into the South.

President Rhee's moods and threats shape each choice in the cables. Staff memos weigh new gear against the risk that he would act alone. The armistice's terms, once a shield, read here as a cage. The record shows an alliance kept in place by aid, patience, and constant talk. Advanced weapons talks dominate the part's files from 1956 onward.
frus-1958-60v07p2:
Western Europe fills Part 2 of Volume VII of the 1958–1960 set, in country blocks. France leads, the longest run, through de Gaulle's return and his push for three-power talks. Atomic sharing with Paris fills long files.

Italy follows, on the opening to the left and missile basing. Spain, Portugal, and the smaller states close the part. Paris visits by both presidents frame the French block. The papers show an ally bent on rank. Each French ask was weighed against the alliance it strained. Missile basing in Italy fills the second long run here.
frus-1958-60v10p2:
Part 2 of Volume X of the 1958–1960 set joins Eastern Europe with Finland, Greece, and Turkey. East-West exchanges lead. Albania and Bulgaria follow, with ties to Sofia resumed in these files.

Poland takes a long run, on aid as a wedge. Yugoslavia appears twice, so central was Tito's course. Finland's files weigh food aid against Soviet pull. Greece closes the part. The record shows the bloc's edges worked one by one. Each small opening was priced, tested, and written up for the next. Greece and Turkey both close the part with aid files.
frus-1964-68v29p2:
Part 2 of Volume XXIX, in the 1964-1968 series, covers Japan in 140 documents. The papers deal with the security treaty, trade, and the return of Okinawa. They also cover textile disputes and Japan's growing weight in Asia. Talks in Tokyo and Washington fill much of the volume. U.S. officials sound out Japanese leaders on treaty review well before it falls due.

Embassy cables report debate inside the Japanese Diet and the ruling party. Memos weigh base rights against trade friction. The records show an alliance shifting as Japan grows richer. By the close, Okinawa and trade dominate the agenda.
frus-1969-76v19p2:
Japan from 1969 to 1972 is the subject of Part 2 of Volume XIX in the 1969-1976 series. The first chapter covers the 1969 decision on the return of Okinawa. The next follows ties after the first Nixon-Sato summit. A third chapter, Change and Reassessment, covers 1971. The shock of the China opening and the dollar crisis falls in this span. The last chapter moves toward a new balance in 1972.

The papers mix summit talk records with cables on trade and textiles. Japan's reserves, grown from $3 billion in 1968 to more than $7 billion, fuel U.S. pressure. The volume traces a partnership under real strain.
frus-1969-76v38p2:
Part 2 of Volume XXXVIII, in the 1969-1976 series, covers the running of foreign policy and public diplomacy from 1973 to 1976. The first chapter treats the intelligence community under inquiry and reform. Later chapters cover information policy, cultural affairs, and the daily management of the State Department. Others treat how the government organized for defense, economic, and global issues. The volume closes with the National Security Council system and the handover from Ford to Carter.

Cables in the middle chapters weigh wider cultural exchange with the Soviet Union under the Helsinki act. Proposals cover newspapers, books, and student swaps. The volume is a record of the machine being rebuilt while it ran.
frus-1969-76ve05p2:
Part 2 of Volume E-5 covers North Africa from 1969 to 1972 in the 1969-1976 series. A first chapter states U.S. policy toward the region. Chapters then follow Algeria, Libya, Morocco, and Tunisia. Libya takes the largest share. Its chapter covers the 1969 coup, the loss of Wheelus Air Base, and the new regime's oil demands. A later report notes Egyptian staff at the old base under Libyan use.

The Algeria chapters deal with strained ties after the 1967 war. Morocco and Tunisia draw smaller, steadier records. The volume shows Washington adjusting to a harder North Africa after 1969.
frus-1969-76ve09p2:
Part 2 of Volume E-9 covers the Middle East region from 1973 to 1976 in the 1969-1976 series. A regional section opens the volume. Sections then treat Kuwait and the Gulf states, Saudi Arabia, and Oman and the Yemens. Saudi Arabia takes by far the largest share. Its papers cover oil prices, arms sales, and the special tie with Washington after the 1973 embargo. A phone record shows a U.S. firm pressing Kissinger over an F-4 sale to Kuwait.

The Gulf chapters follow new wealth and new arms demands. The Yemen chapters treat the border war's wake and Saudi aid to royalists. The volume is the Gulf side of the post-embargo years.
frus-1969-76ve11p2:
South America from 1973 to 1976 fills Part 2 of Volume E-11 in the 1969-1976 series. Sections cover Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela. Chile takes the largest share by far. Its papers run from the 1973 coup through the junta's first years. They cover aid, debt, and human rights charges. A staff note shows Kissinger seeking a Paris Club deal to reschedule Chile's debt.

Brazil's section deals with trade and its nuclear deal with West Germany. Argentina's covers the return of Peronism and its collapse. The volume is a record of a continent turning toward military rule.
frus-1969-76ve14p2:
Part 2 of Volume E-14 covers arms control and nonproliferation from 1973 to 1976 in the 1969-1976 series. Its 218 documents run in one sequence. They follow the SALT II talks and the work of guarding nuclear material. A Kissinger statement of September 23 urges a world accord, through the IAEA, on guarding nuclear stocks against theft. Threshold test limits and peaceful nuclear blasts also appear.

The papers weigh India's 1974 nuclear test and the spread of sensitive technology. Export rules for reactors and fuel take shape in these years. The volume pairs the superpower talks with the wider task of slowing spread.
frus-1969-76ve15p2:
Part 2 of Volume E-15 covers Western Europe from 1973 to 1976 in the 1969-1976 series. A regional section runs to more than 100 documents. Country sections follow for Canada, Portugal, the Nordic countries, Spain, the United Kingdom, West Germany, and France. Portugal's section is long, covering its 1974 revolution and after. One report calls a rumored Azores-based plot to stir revolt in Portugal a pipedream.

The Spain section covers the last Franco years and the change that followed. Britain's covers entry into the European Community and money strain. The volume gives the allied side of a shifting decade.
frus-1977-80v17p2:
Part 2 of Volume XVII, in the 1977-1980 series, gathers documents on Sub-Saharan Africa. Sections cover the region as a whole, then West, Central, and East Africa. The papers deal with aid, trade, and the new states' money troubles. A report on Liberia ties its calm to solving a near-term fiscal crisis. Fuel and food imports depended on that fix, the report says. Investor trust would decide the longer term.

Other cables cover Nigeria's weight in West Africa and Zaire's crises in Central Africa. The East Africa section deals with Tanzania, Kenya, and Uganda under Amin. The volume gives the quieter half of Carter-era Africa policy.
